sentences.text: Bone fusion in the holotype indicates this was a mature adult weighing 0.31 kg, with a sternum that is proportionally axially long.
It possesses proportionally long ossified uncinate processes fused to the dorsal ribs and exhibits the arctometatarsalian condition in its foot.

The articulated tail features elongated rod-like extensions and chevrons reaching almost to the anterior caudal vertebrae, while five left sternal ribs are preserved, a number exceeding that seen in related genera.
Despite its small size of 0.31 kg, bone fusion confirms it was a fully mature adult.
Five left sternal ribs are preserved, which is more than observed in related genera like Microraptor and Sinornithosaurus.
Zhongjianosaurus was first reported in 2009 from lake deposits in Sihedang, western Liaoning, China, based on a partial postcranial articulated skeleton.
The genus and species were first described by Xu Xing and Qin Zi-Chuan.
The name honors Yang Zhongjian, the founder of Chinese vertebrate paleontology.
The holotype specimen, IVPP V 22775, is housed at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.
Researchers suggest Zhongjianosaurus was possibly omnivorous and arboreal due to its small size.
The discovery of Zhongjianosaurus in the Yixian Formation alongside eight other dromaeosaurids suggests there was sufficient niche partitioning available.
Zhongjianosaurus is classified as a dromaeosaurid belonging to the Microraptoria, a placement supported by synapomorphies and cladistic analyses.
However, some studies suggest an alternate classification for Zhongjianosaurus as an avialan.
Zhongjianosaurus is believed to come from the middle of the Jehol Biota in the Yixian Formation and lived between 125 and 121 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous in what is now Asia.
Specifically, it lived during the Aptian stage, from 121.4 to 113.2 million years ago.
There is a debate regarding finger identification, with the authors proposing digits two, three, and four while most researchers identify them as one, two, and three.
